newsitem.title: USA: GM parts negotiations continue past deadline.
newsitem.headline: GM parts negotiations continue past deadline.

text.p: In encouraging signs for General Motors Corp.'s labour troubles, bargainers met past a strike deadline at a key Wisconsin parts plant Friday after talks to end a Michigan truck plant strike continued through the night for the first time in more than seven weeks.

Bargainers for GM and the United Auto Workers continued talks aimed at a new local agreement for GM's Oak Creek, Wis., catalytic converter plant after an 11:59 p.m. EDT Thursday strike deadline expired.
But the world's largest automaker still faces strike deadlines at two other parts plants in Michigan that are set to expire at 11:59 p.m. EDT Friday.
The Oak Creek talks continued until 3 a.m., then resumed at about 10:30 a.m. Friday, said Kenneth Cameron, a spokesman for GM's Delphi Energy and Engine Management Systems division.

The plant near Milwaukee makes exhaust system catalytic converters for nearly all of GM's North American cars and trucks, as well as customers in Europe and Asia. A work stoppage at the 870-employee factory would begin to halt production at most of GM's 29 North American car and truck assembly plants within days, GM officials say.
Cameron declined to characterise the progress of the talks but said the deadline extension was encouraging.
"Obviously, there had to be some reason to continue, and presumably there was some progress being made," he said.
At GM's Pontiac, Mich., truck assembly plant and related facilities, bargainers met all night Thursday for the first time since 5,800 workers walked off the job on April 22.

Until this week, talks have moved slowly at the plant, which is one of three that produce GM's popular full-size Chevrolet and GMC pickup trucks. Some analysts view the Oak Creek strike threat and the Friday night strike deadlines in Michigan as moves by the UAW to pressure GM into settling the Pontiac walkout.

About 900 workers at a GM foundry in Saginaw, Mich., and 2,346 hourly workers at a metal stamping plant in Grand Rapids, Mich., are set to walk off the job at 11:59 p.m. EDT unless new local agreements for those plants are reached.

The Saginaw plant makes pistons, piston rods and transmission parts for a variety of GM vehicles, while the Grand Rapids plant stamps out doors, fenders, hoods and other sheet metal parts for various cars and trucks, including GM's all-new minivans.
The impact from possible strikes at the Michigan plants is expected to be less severe than a strike at the Wisconsin plant would be.

At Oak Creek, UAW Local 1866 is demanding new restrictions on GM's ability to shift work to outside suppliers as well as a long-term commitment from GM that it will continue to invest in its catalytic converter business. Future air pollution restrictions are expected to require a new generation of more complex precious-metal catalysts.

At Pontiac and the other plants, the major issue is staffing levels -- the union wants GM to hire more new workers to replace retirees and compensate for increased production line speeds. UAW Local 594 in Pontiac, for example, started with a demand for about 600 new workers.
GM has resisted, in part because a new-generation pickup truck due next year is expected to require about 30 percent fewer workers to build it.
"Our feelings are that General Motors must realise we're determined to end the unjust treatment of our people," said Jim Abare, an officer of Local 594. "We're not going to back down."
GM's stock was up 62.5 cents at $57.625 in midday trading on the New York Stock Exchange.
